 Here's what to know
 • Trump heads to Asia: At two leaders summits — in Manila and Shenzhen — President Donald Trump will look to counter the narrative of his declining power at home. The Iran war, along with Trump’s efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine , are likely to hang over the talks in Asia, where fuel prices have spiked due to the conflicts.
 • Historic trilateral: His trip includes an unprecedented meeting with the authoritarian leaders of China and Russia , where Trump said he will discuss the war in Ukraine . Trump also said he “may meet” with Kim Jong Un , should the North Korean leader also make an appearance in China this week.
 • Semiconductor scandal looms: Trump said he “might” discuss Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s reported affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset in his separate one-on-one meeting with Xi.

 Even abroad, Trump can’t get away from data center protests
 By Kathleen Magramo 
 President Donald Trump will arrive in the Philippines to protests against data centers planned in the country as part of a US-led plan to dominate AI.
 The Philippines is one of 26 signatories of Pax Silica, a US State Department-led initiative to lure AI-related industries away from Chinese supply chains.
 But there is growing anger in the country over plans to build a 1,620 hectare technology hub near a former American military base in Luzon as part of the project.
 The hub will be built in Capas, Tarlac, which was the endpoint of the “death march” of Filipino and American prisoners of war during World War II. It is also home to indigenous peoples called the Aeta, who traveled to the capital Manila to protest possibly being displaced from their ancestral lands.
 Protesters opposing the knock-on economic impacts from the US-Iran war and the US-led Pax Silica initiative clashed with police in the Philippines ahead of the ASEAN summit on Sunday. More than 200 people were arrested, according to police.

 Trump advisers battling over China policy are all joining his trip to Asia
 By Kevin Liptak in Manila
 An open divide among President Donald Trump’s advisers over China has burst into public view this week. That could make for an awkward flight aboard Air Force One, where many of the warring advisers have been sequestered now for hours.
 Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are all accompanying Trump as he makes the nearly 20-hour journey from Washington to Manila.
 Bessent recently publicly heaped blame on Lutnick’s department for slow-walking new restrictions on AI technology going to China, claiming the rest of the president’s advisers all favored tighter rules.
 It underscored an internal debate that has been roiling the administration for months. The scandal involving Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has thrust the issue into the foreground.
 Trump appeared to defend Lutnick as he was departing the White House, saying he was looking to avoid confrontation with Beijing.
 “One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China,” Trump said on the South Lawn. “Both are acceptable, but they’re different views.”

 Before tech talks with China, US fires first with new restrictions on chip exports
 By Stephanie Yang 
 Now former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks during a doorstep after attending the AI Ecosystem Reception in Tokyo, Japan, July 16. 
 Manami Yamada/Reuters 
 At their last meeting, President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping seemed ready to back away from confrontation amid an escalating tech rivalry, and even potentially collaborate on AI development safeguards.
 The Nvidia scandal could end all that.
 Days before Trump is set to meet Xi in Shenzhen, the US Commerce Department increased restrictions on exports of advanced US semiconductors in an effort to further limit China’s access to them.
 The measures announced Monday will apply to overseas data centers that supply “significant volumes” of computing power to a list of countries including China, and require new licenses for exports to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, due to a “higher-than-normal risk” of diversion, or rerouting chips to unauthorized buyers.
 The rule change follows growing controversy over Nvidia, the world’s biggest supplier of advanced AI chips, and its sales to a Singapore-based company Megaspeed that is under investigation for potentially diverting server shipments to China.
 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after reports he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US officials suspected of being part of an intelligence operation by China.
 Beijing has called the allegations groundless and an attempt to smear China. But the scandal has bolstered US efforts to strengthen tech export controls, which could derail recent efforts to ease trade tensions or even provoke retaliation from China.
 At a press briefing on Tuesday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said Beijing “will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
 Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said the new restrictions were “a typical case of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction. It runs counter to the consensus reached by both sides.”

 Trump says he “may meet” with Kim Jong Un in China
 By Lex Harvey 
 US President Donald Trump meets with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un at the demilitarized zone separating the two Koreas, in Panmunjom, South Korea, June 30, 2019. 
 Kevin Lamarque/Reuters/File 
 US President Donald Trump said he “may meet” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his visit to China, adding that it would be up to Beijing’s leader Xi Jinping.
 “We might have Kim Jong Un. He may come. I don’t know. That’s up to President Xi,” Trump told reporters as he left the White House on Monday.
 Trump is traveling to Shenzhen, China later this week to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting, where he plans to hold trilateral talks with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
 Trump has repeatedly said he wishes to meet with the North Korean leader. North Korea is not a member of APEC and Kim has not confirmed any plans to attend the summit. At a news briefing Tuesday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said he had no information on whether Kim would attend APEC this week.
 Kim’s travel habits could make an impromptu meeting difficult. The leader is known to travel on a heavily armored train that reportedly travels at an average speed of 37 miles per hour. Shenzhen is more than 1,000 miles from the North Korean border.
 Kim took a 2.5 day train journey across China to meet Trump in Hanoi, Vietnam in 2019.

 Canada and China announce new trade deal in further sign of deepening ties
 By Lex Harvey 
 Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney attends a bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting on November 17 in Shenzhen, China. 
 Maxim Shemetov/Pool/Getty Images 
 Ottawa and Beijing announced a new trade deal Tuesday as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Chinese leader Xi Jinping met in Shenzhen, in a further sign of deepening ties amid Canada’s trade friction with the United States.
 “Canada and China have recalibrated our relationship to the benefit of citizens in both countries,” Carney said in a news release Tuesday.
 “Canada is building our strength at home and diversifying our relationships abroad so that we have the freedom to live our lives as we choose.”
 China has agreed to relieve tariffs on about 400 million Canadian dollars ($280 million) worth of Canadian pork and seafood exports, while Canada agreed to extend remission measures for Chinese steel and aluminum products where Canadian supply is insufficient and unavailable, according to the Canadian government statement published Tuesday.
 Canada also plans to launch a new major trade mission to China in 2027, it said. China is Canada’s second largest trading partner after the US, and trade between the two countries exceeded 125 billion Canadian dollars ($87.4 billion) in 2025.
 “Improving and developing China-Canada relations serves the interests of the peoples of both countries and is also conducive to safeguarding world peace and stability and promoting development and prosperity,” Xi told Carney Tuesday during their meeting, according to Chinese state media.
 Historically one of the world’s closest economic partnerships, Canada and the US have been locked in a trade war during President Donald Trump’s second term. Carney has moved to lessen his country’s reliance on the US, forging closer economic ties with Europe and Asia.
 During his meeting with Xi, Carney hailed the “greater predictability and stability” in Canada-China relations following his trip to Beijing in January where the leaders announced a new “strategic partnership” and agreed to ease longstanding trade tensions.

 Why is Trump heading to the Philippines?
 By Kathleen Magramo and Helen Regan 
 US President Donald Trump departs the White House on November 16 in Washington, DC. 
 Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images 
 US President Donald Trump is the last leader expected to land in Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit on Tuesday, two days after the event kicked off.
 Trump will attend the US-ASEAN Special Summit scheduled that evening local time, which a Filipino diplomat said would be “the last engagement to cap the meetings on 17 November.”
 So, why is Trump bothering to make an appearance at all? Well, his attendance underscores Washington’s desire to engage with the economic bloc as part of its efforts to counter growing Chinese influence in the Asia-Pacific region.
 ASEAN’s 11 member countries are a motley bunch. They include US allies Thailand and the Philippines, military-ruled Myanmar, communist-run Vietnam and Laos and economic giant – and the world’s most populous Muslim nation – Indonesia.
 Another member is the wealthy city-state of Singapore, currently under global spotlight over Megaspeed , a company based there that US officials suspect was at the center of a shadow industry of complex transactions and shell companies that facilitated chip smuggling to China.
 There’s plenty on ASEAN’s agenda at the Manila summit: from rising fuel prices sparked by the US and Israel’s war with Iran, to toxic smog in the region.
 Trump will meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr as well as the leaders of the other three so-called “Quad” countries: India, Japan and Australia. The Quad is an informal strategic forum focused on the region, featuring summits, information exchanges and military drills.

 President Donald Trump said Monday that he’s not considering replacing Commerce Secretary Howard Luntick, even as scrutiny intensifies over whether he should have done more to limit the sale of advanced chips to China.
 Trump downplayed reported disagreements between Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, saying that the two men “have two different views” over whether the Commerce Department should have moved faster in labeling Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat.

 In a tense Situation Room meeting earlier this month, Bessent challenged Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to blacklist Megaspeed.

 Trump’s Nvidia dilemma follows him to China 
 1:16
 The scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s high-powered AI chips and reported affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset will loom over Donald Trump’s visit to Shenzhen, the hub of China’s tech industry, even though the president’s aides insist it wouldn’t dominate the journey.
 Huang resigned from Nvidia after reports of multiple affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with Alice Huang, whom US officials fear could be working with Chinese intelligence. Alice Huang was an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed , an Nvidia customer under investigation for potentially diverting highly coveted US semiconductors to entities in China in violation of US export controls.
 Trump said he “might” discuss Alice Huang with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. US officials previously told CNN that they did not expect Trump to bring up the scandal.
 In an earlier exchange with reporters surrounding Nvidia, Trump offered a glimpse of his posture ahead of the meeting with Xi: Not rocking the boat.
 “We’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” Trump said.
 Officials said they also did not expect the two men to discuss the newly revived debate inside the administration over how to further restrict high-powered chips from going to China .
 Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was expected to join the president on the trip, and officials have not indicated those plans have changed amid the Nvidia scandal, which has seen Lutnick face intense scrutiny for what some Trump advisers see as inaction in placing limits on US chip exports to China.

 Trump's meeting with Xi and Putin will be historic
 By Kevin Liptak 
 President of the People's Republic of China Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. 
 Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump will meet jointly with China’s leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, a first-ever trilateral sit-down between the leaders of the three countries.
 The meeting will focus on nuclear nonproliferation, a topic Trump has said he believes could yield a new agreement between the world’s biggest nuclear-armed states.
 While their trilateral is unprecedented, separately, the leaders have a wealth of history.
 Xi has met with Putin dozens of times. The pair have built a close alliance, bound by ties that run deep between their nations. China has claimed neutrality in the war and sought to position itself as a peace broker. But NATO allies believe it has been instrumental in Russia’s effort to defeat Ukraine, providing Moscow with equipment to support weapon assembly, and contributing technology and imagery.
 Trump and Putin have met in person seven times. The two leaders’ relationship has been tumultuous but appears to have strengthened in recent months. Trump faced a barrage of criticism in October when he suspended fuel export sanctions on Russia for at least six months, allowing Putin to release diesel into the global energy market at a time when US fuel prices were skyrocketing.

 How Trump is hoping to use his trip to Asia
 By Kevin Liptak 
 President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before walking to board Marine One as departs from the South Lawn of the White House on November 16. 
 Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images 
 It’s a time-tested tradition: Presidents looking to reassert authority and escape political gloom head overseas for a global pick-me-up.
 President Donald Trump will attempt to follow suit with a long-planned trip through Asia, punctuated Thursday by an unprecedented three-way meeting with authoritarian leaders from China and Russia .
 Comparisons with a newly constrained US leader may be unavoidable.
 The sharp rebuke Trump faced from voters this month was quickly clocked by his foreign counterparts, all watching closely for signs of fading political capital and early-onset lame-duck status.
 At two leaders summits — the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) in Shenzhen — Trump will look to counter the narrative of his declining power.
 Trump has spent the past year working to cultivate deeper ties Xi. And he’s been seeking new trade deals, with plans to sign an agreement with Thailand this week, White House officials said.
 Yet the Iran war, along with Trump’s efforts to end the war in Ukraine , continue to dominate his foreign policy agenda. Both are likely to hang over his talks in Asia, where fuel prices have spiked due to the conflicts.
 So, too, will Democrats’ stateside victories lead to questions of just how much Trump has left to offer. His two signature foreign policy initiatives — global tariffs and the Iran war — led to price increases that propelled voter anger toward him and Republicans. Democrats have vowed to limit his authorities on both, challenging the long-held adage that a president has a freer hand on foreign matters.
